title: edge-routing-and-tenancy-modes-ops-notes
content:
Purpose
This note collects practical patterns and trade-offs for tenant routing across Hosted, Dedicated and Private modes. The goal is an operations-friendly matrix that platform teams and SREs can use when designing routing policies, isolation boundaries, and multi-region failover.

Executive summary (TL;DR)
- Hosted: multi-tenant control plane, shared data plane pools, lightweight per-tenant policy => best for rapid scale and cost efficiency but requires strict soft-isolation, request-level policy enforcement, and strong observability.
- Dedicated: isolated serving pools per tenant (physically or logically partitioned GPUs), shared control plane or split control plane, predictable performance/SLA; routing focuses on capacity-aware placement and tenant-aware affinity.
- Private: customer-managed control plane or hybrid control plane with customer-controlled data plane (VPC/on-prem). Strongest isolation and compliance guarantees; routing is constrained by network topologies and customer routing rules, often requiring collocated control-plane proxies or edge connectors.

Key concepts and terminology
- Control plane: orchestration, policy decision, model catalog, routing policy repository, rollout orchestration.
- Data plane: inference-serving hosts (GPUs/TPUs), ingress/egress proxies, model artifacts.
- PIP (Policy Enforcement Point): the component applying routing decisions (ingress proxy, edge router, L7 gateway).
- PDP (Policy Decision Point): component that computes route based on tenant, model, region, capacity, SLAs, security posture.
- Tenant affinity / sticky routing: binding a tenant to a pool or node to preserve cache, KV state, or warm workers.

Routing primitives (what we use to build policies)
- Region preference: prefer local region when latency-critical, else fallback to warm-writable region.
- Capacity tiering: route to dedicated pool first (if the tenant has enough reserved capacity), then to hosted shared pools, then to overflow pools in another region.
- Variant fallback: if preferred model variant is unavailable, route to compatible quantized or smaller variant.
- Isolation gate: a boolean that blocks routing to any non-isolated pool for tenants with compliance requirements.
- Affinity window: duration for which sticky routing is preserved (e.g., 5 minutes for KV cache reuse).

Differences by deployment mode (detailed)
1) Hosted (multi-tenant data plane)
- Isolation model: logical isolation (namespaces, tenant ids, per-request metadata). No dedicated hardware by default.
- PDP/PIP placement: PDP lives in control plane (hosted); PIP at edge/ingress proxy (hosted infra).
- Failure model: noisy neighbors possible; mitigation by autoscaling, throttles, and priority queuing.
- Routing policy examples: route based on token-tier, enforce per-tenant rate limits at PIP, prefer region-local pooled instances to keep latency low.
- Observability: token-level traces, per-tenant tail-latency histograms, per-model quality deltas.
- Pros: cost effective, easy onboarding, single catalog.
- Cons: weaker hardware isolation, requires hardened multi-tenant safeguards, more complex SLO enforcement.

2) Dedicated (reserved pools)
- Isolation model: strong logical isolation and frequently physical isolation (separate nodes/pools); can be host-affinity or pool-per-tenant.
- PDP/PIP placement: PDP may remain in a shared control plane or be colocated with dedicated region control proxies for latency; PIP usually deploys in front of dedicated pool and enforces tenant-only traffic.
- Failure model: predictable performance; capacity exhaustion -> queue or borrow from hosted overflow (if policy allows).
- Routing policy examples: always route tenant X to its reserved pool unless it is at >85% utilization, then either queue or spill-over to a cold hosted pool with reduced model variant.
- Observability: dedicated dashboards, head-of-line protection metrics, reserved-utilization alerts.
- Pros: predictable latency, compliance-friendly, easier SLA guarantees.
- Cons: higher cost, more complex provisioning.

3) Private (VPC / on-prem)
- Isolation model: customer-managed network and compute. Control plane options: fully customer control plane (air-gapped) or hybrid where Redwood control plane issues signed manifests and customer data plane pulls.
- PDP/PIP placement: PDP can be pushed as policy bundles; PIP typically lives inside the customer VPC (sidecar/ingress).
- Failure model: constrained by customer network; cross-region routing may be blocked or require explicit peering.
- Routing policy examples: local-only routing by default, with explicit permission to send buffered requests to Redwood-hosted overflow via secure tunnel.
- Observability: audit-focus (who/what requested), KMS-backed keying for models, and customer log sinks.
- Pros: strongest compliance and data isolation.
- Cons: slower iteration, network constraints, and more ops burden on customer.

Isolation boundary patterns (practical templates)
- Pattern A: Logical namespace + PIP label enforcement (Hosted)
  Use tenant id + request metadata tags. PDP stores policies per-tenant. PIP rejects requests that attempt to cross tenant id boundaries. Good for small customers and cost-sensitive tenants.
- Pattern B: Pool-per-tenant with overflow (Dedicated)
  Dedicated pools that accept only tenant-signed tokens. Overflow routes to shared pools with reduced priority and different telemetry.
- Pattern C: Edge connector with push/pull policies (Private hybrid)
  Customer runs an edge connector that exposes a local API and pulls signed model manifests from control plane. Control plane issues revocation lists and signed policy bundles.

Multi-region considerations
- Data residency policies must be expressed as first-class constraints in PDP (e.g., do-not-leave-region, region-preference weight).
- Cold-starts vs. pre-warmed pools: for multi-region, maintain warm pools in adjacent regions for critical tenants; use affinity windows to improve hit-rates.
- Failover ordering: region-local dedicated -> region-local shared -> cross-region dedicated -> cross-region shared. Configure different SLAs for each step.
- Network egress costs: when routing cross-region, include estimated egress cost in PDP scoring to avoid surprises for cost-sensitive customers.

Observability and SLO enforcement
- Tag every routing decision with: tenant_id, policy_id, route_path, decision_time, and PDP_score. Store in trace logs.
- Real-time policy violations stream to a dedicated alerting pipeline (e.g., policy-breach topic).
- Add per-tenant rolling SLOs for p95 latency and model quality; trigger automatic rollback of routing changes that increase error rates.

Security & compliance enforcement hooks
- Mutual TLS and per-tenant certs for dedicated/private pools.
- Signed manifests and short-lived capability tokens for private edge connectors.
- KMS/HSM integration for model keys and telemetry masking.

Operational playbook snippets
- On noisy neighbor detection in Hosted: immediately reduce concurrency weight for offending tenant, shift burst traffic to cold overflow pool, open incident with tenant owner.
- On dedicated pool exhaustion: throttle non-critical endpoints, inform sales/CS for capacity expansion, optionally enable spillover to shared pool after consent.
- Cross-region outage: if remote region unavailable, enable region-preference failover to next nearest region; if customer enforced do-not-leave-region, degrade with 503 and clear message.

Decision matrix (short)
- If customer requires hardware isolation + strict SLO -> Dedicated (pool-per-tenant).
- If customer requires data residency + customer-managed keys -> Private.
- If customer needs rapid onboarding, low-cost and flexible scaling -> Hosted.

Open questions / next steps
- Policy language: adopt a compact DSL for PDP rules so product and infra can author policies without redeploys. Prototype rule syntax by Q2.
- Affinity consistency: evaluate distributed sticky routing implementation vs central PDP with short-lived leases.
- Cost-aware PDP scoring: integrate cost signals (e.g., egress, spot-vs-on-demand) into runtime scoring.

Notes to reviewers
- This is operational-first: if you see gaps between policy language and actual PIP implementation, call out concrete PoC steps.
- I intentionally kept examples concrete (percent utilization, affinity windows) — please challenge numbers with real telemetry during review.
